text: Finished the last coat of paint on the balcony railing this afternoon and just stood there grinning. The whole evening smelled of fresh paint and chai, and I kept finding excuses to walk past it. Honestly, I haven't enjoyed a chore this much in years.

The landlord kept my deposit again and blamed it on normal wear, even after I sent photos of every room. I read his message three times with my jaw clenched. How dare he treat us like we can't read our own lease? I typed a reply, deleted it, and typed a sharper one.

My heart was racing the whole drive to the clinic. Every time the phone buzzed I flinched, sure it was the doctor calling with something terrible. I keep running through the worst scenarios even though nobody has told me anything is wrong yet.

I handed Meera the spare key and my account passwords before leaving for two weeks, and I didn't even think twice. She has never once let me down. Whatever happens while I'm gone, I know she'll handle it exactly the way I would.

Cleared out Dad's side of the wardrobe today. His old grey sweater still held a faint smell of him, and I sat on the floor holding it for a long time. The house feels hollow in a way I can't describe to anyone.

Opened the office fridge and found a container of something that had grown a furry green coat and was leaking onto the shelf. The smell hit me like a wall and I nearly gagged. I could not bring myself to touch it, even with gloves.

The tickets are booked and I keep checking the countdown on my phone. Twelve days until the mountain trek, and I've already laid out my boots and thermal layers on the bed. I can't wait to see what the trail looks like at sunrise.

Watching my little sister fall asleep on the couch with her sketchbook still on her lap, I felt so tender toward her. I pulled a blanket over her and tucked her hair back. She's my favourite person in the world, and I hope she knows it.

Sent out my twentieth job application this month, and I already know how this will go. Nobody has even replied to the first nineteen. Nothing about the market suggests this one will be different, so I'm not bothering to expect anything.

I opened the door expecting the delivery guy and found my old college roommate standing there with a suitcase. I actually yelled out loud. Six years without a word, and she just turned up in the rain like it was nothing. I still can't process it.

The first round of tests came back inconclusive, but the doctor sounded sure about the next steps. I've got a good feeling about this treatment. Things are going to get better by spring, and I can already picture myself back on the cricket field.

I assumed the quiz would be brutal, so when the professor handed back my paper with a top mark I stared at it twice. Wait, that can't be my name on this. I checked the neighbour's sheet just to make sure it wasn't a mix-up.

The group chat went quiet after Arjun moved to Pune. Nobody says it, but we've all drifted apart. I scrolled through our old photos tonight and felt a heavy ache, like something that mattered had quietly slipped away without a goodbye.

Money is tight this month, but I started a small savings jar and a plan for the freelance work. If I keep this up, I think we'll be out of the red by December. It feels doable, and I'm more hopeful than I've been in ages.

Third night this week the neighbour's generator ran past midnight. I banged on the wall and got nothing back. I'm sick of being polite about it; my sleep is wrecked and nobody seems to care. Tomorrow I'm filing a formal complaint.

Mum called just to ask whether I'd eaten, like she always does. I stayed on the line longer than usual because her voice made me feel warm all over. I adore how she worries about the smallest things and never gets tired of me.

We danced in the kitchen for no reason this evening, flour all over the counter and the music far too loud. My cheeks hurt from laughing. Days like this are the ones I want to remember, just plain good fun.

There was a man standing outside my building when I came home late, and he didn't move when I walked past. My hands were shaking as I fumbled for the keys. I locked the door, checked it twice, and sat in the dark listening for footsteps.

They say the new management will turn things around, but I've watched three of these restructures already. The same problems come back every time. I don't expect our team to survive the year, whatever the slides promise.

When the contractor said the wiring would be done by Friday, I believed him; he's been straight with us from day one. I didn't ask for receipts or hover around the site. I know his word is solid, and that counts for a lot with me.
The new pottery class starts Monday. I've bought the clay, sketched three bowl designs, and I'm itching to get my hands on the wheel again. I can't wait to see what comes out of the kiln this time.

The public restroom at the station was filthy, the floor sticky and a stench that made my stomach turn. I held my breath and left without washing my hands. I still feel repulsed just thinking about it.

I told my brother about the loan before I told anyone else. He listened without judging and said he'd go through the papers with me. I know he'll be honest and I can lean on him, which is exactly why he was the first person I called.

A colleague sneezed straight into the shared salad bowl and then just kept serving. I felt my skin crawl. I put my plate down and couldn't eat anything else at that lunch; the thought alone made me feel sick.

I keep telling myself the exam prep is going fine, but my practice scores haven't moved in a month. Realistically, I won't clear the cutoff. There's no use pretending otherwise, so I'm just going through the motions until the date arrives.
Got to the beach at dawn with my cousins and spent the entire morning in the waves. Salt in my hair, sand in everything, and I was laughing so much my stomach hurt. I could have stayed there all day.
Seven days to go until the book fair opens in town. I've made a list of the stalls to hit first and cleared a shelf at home. I'm genuinely eager to see what rare titles turn up this year.

The plane dropped suddenly and my stomach lurched; I gripped the armrest until my knuckles whitened. I kept staring at the flight attendants for any sign they were worried. Even after we levelled out I couldn't make my breathing slow down.

He interrupted me in the meeting for the fourth time and then presented my idea as his own. I kept my face still, but inside I was seething. I'm tired of being steamrolled and I'm not letting it slide this time.
The garden looks bare now, but the seedlings are strong and the forecast is good. I'm convinced we'll have tomatoes by summer. With a little patience, I think the whole plot will fill out nicely.

Her empty chair at dinner was the hardest part. We kept setting four plates out of habit, and nobody said anything. I swallowed hard and pushed my food around, missing her laugh more than I can put into words.

I've loved my grandmother's handwriting for as long as I can remember. Today I found a recipe card in her looping script and held it close to my chest. Everything about her feels so dear to me, even a grocery list.

I had no idea the old cinema was being turned into a library until I walked past and saw shelves through the glass. I stopped dead on the pavement. Last month it was boarded up! Nobody told me a thing.
I haven't opened the credit card statement in two weeks because I dread what the total is. My chest tightens every time the notification pops up. What if I really can't cover it this month?
Priya fell asleep on my shoulder during the train ride, and I didn't move for an hour even though my arm went numb. I just wanted to keep her there. I'm so fond of her it's almost silly.

The wedding is Saturday and I'm counting the hours until I can see my whole extended family under one roof. I've already picked my outfit and packed the gift. I'm eagerly waiting for the music and the food.

I got home to find the whole flat rearranged, and I actually gasped. The sofa was under the window, my desk was in a different corner, and there was a note from my flatmate saying she'd explain later. I never saw that coming.

The airline lost my bag and then the desk clerk shrugged and told me to fill out a form online. I was furious. Two days of calls, and everyone just passes me along. I'm done being polite with people who don't care.

My supervisor said she would back me in front of the committee, and I know she will. In four years she has never gone back on a promise. I walked into that review feeling steady purely because of her word.

Finally nailed the guitar solo after weeks of fumbling. I played it six times straight just to hear it come out clean. This is the best I've felt about anything all month, and I was grinning like a fool.

Watched the movers carry the last box out of our old flat and just felt empty. Twelve years of birthdays and arguments and ordinary Tuesdays in those rooms. I locked the door and sat in the car for a while, unable to start it.

I found a hair in my soup and the waiter just shrugged. The sight of it floating there turned my stomach, and I pushed the bowl away. I couldn't even look at the food anymore; the whole idea was revolting.

The interview didn't feel perfect, but the panel seemed interested, and they asked about start dates. I think I'm in with a real shot. Whatever happens, I'm confident the year ahead holds something good for me.

Another committee, another round of promises. I've sat through enough of these to know nothing will change on the village road. They'll talk, they'll take photos, and the potholes will outlast us all.
My knee is still stiff, but the physio says I'm ahead of schedule. I can see myself jogging again by spring, maybe even running the local 10K. I feel good about where this is heading.
I don't think the shop will last past winter. Sales dropped again and the rent is going up. I keep crunching numbers hoping for a different answer, but every version ends the same way.

Someone left a bag of rotting garbage in the stairwell for days, and the smell crept into the whole building. Passing it every morning made me retch. I hold my sleeve over my nose and hurry by, appalled that anyone could live like that.

Rain tapped on the window while Rohan hummed to himself and made tea, and I realised how deeply I care about him. Just the sound of him puttering around the kitchen makes me feel at home. I wanted to hug him from behind and never let go.
My cousin's baby laughed for the first time today and the whole room erupted. I couldn't stop smiling for an hour afterwards. Such a small thing, and yet it lit up the entire afternoon.

A stranger on the bus handed me my wallet, which I hadn't even noticed was missing. Cash and cards, all there. I just stood there blinking, completely lost for words, and then the bus pulled away before I could say anything.
I got the rejection letter from the programme today. I'd been so sure. I closed the laptop and lay on the floor looking at the ceiling, feeling the disappointment settle in my chest like a stone.
I keep hearing footsteps in the attic at night. I tell myself it's the pipes, but I lie rigid under the covers with the lights on, listening. I can't shake the dread that something is up there.

Our first road trip as a couple starts tomorrow morning. I've made a playlist, planned the stops, and I'm buzzing at the thought of the open highway. I'm eager to find out what the coast looks like at golden hour.

I let the new mechanic keep the car overnight without a second thought. My neighbour has used him for years and swears by his honesty. I believe it; he strikes me as someone who tells you the truth even when it costs him.
My teammate skipped the group call again and left me to cover his section. I was so frustrated I slammed the laptop shut. This is the third time he's pulled this, and nobody ever calls him out.

The seed catalogue arrived and I've circled half of it. Spring planting is still months off, but I'm already laying out the beds in my head and itching to get my hands in the soil. I can't wait for the first warm weekend.
When Dev said he'd pick up the kids from school, I stopped thinking about it entirely. He's the one person I can count on without checking in. I let the whole afternoon go by knowing it was handled.
I had no clue my team had organised a farewell cake. I walked into the meeting room and everybody yelled. My mouth just hung open; I honestly thought it was a routine status call.
I started a new diet plan again, but I already know I'll quit by next week. I've done this cycle too many times. There's no point pretending this will be the one that sticks.

The meat at the market stall was crawling with flies, and the vendor kept wiping the counter with a filthy rag. My stomach heaved. I'll never buy anything from that place again; I can't even picture eating it.
They scheduled my shift over my day off after I'd already told them twice. I stared at the roster, fuming. It feels like my time means nothing to them, and I'm done swallowing it quietly.

I've been learning Spanish for three months, and today I held a short conversation with the neighbour. It's slow progress, but I'm certain that by next year I'll be fluent enough to travel. Things are moving the right way.
Won the neighbourhood quiz night with a last-minute guess, and my team lifted me off the ground. I can't remember the last time I laughed so hard. It was a perfect, silly evening.
I stood at the door of my daughter's room and watched her sleep, one arm flung over her stuffed rabbit. My heart felt too full. I'd do anything for that kid, and I told her so in a whisper.
Presentation tomorrow at nine and my mouth is already dry. I keep imagining blanking out in front of everyone. I rehearsed until midnight, but the tight knot in my stomach hasn't loosened at all.
The shop where Grandpa used to buy me sweets has closed for good. I walked by, looked at the shuttered window, and felt a lump rise in my throat. A piece of my childhood is gone.
I didn't get invited to the trip. Nobody said it directly; I just saw the photos online later. I put my phone face down and sat in the quiet, feeling left behind and hurt.
The lump the doctor found might be nothing, but waiting for the biopsy is making me jittery. I can't concentrate at work and I keep checking my phone. What if the result is the one I don't want?
Spent the afternoon baking with my nieces, and everything turned out slightly lopsided and delicious. We ate warm cookies straight off the tray. I haven't had this much fun in ages.
The new bus route starts next month, which should cut my commute in half. I think this will change my days for the better. Things are looking up, and I'm sure I'll finally find time for the gym.
I showed the presentation to my mentor first. She said it was ready, and that's good enough for me. She's never steered me wrong, so I'll go with her judgment and not second-guess it.
Four more sleeps until the lantern festival. I've been scrolling through pictures of last year's lights and plotting where we'll stand to watch. I'm itching for the night to arrive.
I doubt the repair will hold. The plumber patched it with tape last time, and it leaked within a week. I'm already bracing for the flood; this house will keep falling apart no matter what we do.
I was certain the box held books, but when I lifted the lid there was a tiny puppy staring up at me. I made a noise I've never made before. I could barely process what I was looking at.
The driver cut across two lanes and nearly clipped my bike, then glared at me like I was the problem. My hands were shaking with rage. I shouted something I won't repeat here.
The hostel bathroom had hair clogging the drain and a smell like rotten eggs. I retched at the doorway. Just seeing the black slime on the tiles made my skin crawl, and I left without showering.
Every Sunday my grandfather teaches me a new card trick, and I treasure those hours more than he knows. His hands, his teasing grin, the way he calls me kiddo, I adore all of it.

I wrote a long message to my best friend about how much she means to me, and I smiled the whole time I typed. She's been there through everything. I'm so lucky to have someone I care about this deeply.
Studio tour next week! I've been looking forward to this ever since the invite arrived. I've read up on the director and drafted a list of questions to ask. Counting down the days.

The bank manager walked me through every clause without rushing, and I felt at ease signing. He's handled my family's accounts for decades. I believe he has our interests at heart, so I didn't hesitate for a second.

I found my old school uniform in the loft and sat holding it. Those years felt so far away from who I've become. A heaviness settled over me for the rest of the evening, and I missed the person I used to be.
I don't see how the team can make the deadline. We lost two people and the scope hasn't shrunk. Everyone keeps saying we'll manage, but I'm convinced it ends in a missed launch and a long apology.
My sister's recovery is going better than the doctors expected. I'm certain she'll be home soon, and we'll look back on this as a bad chapter that ended well. Good days are coming; I can feel it.
A man spat on the pavement right beside me, and I recoiled. The sound alone made my stomach turn. I walked three blocks out of my way to avoid the spot, still grimacing.
I haven't slept since the storm warning. The river is already high and the water keeps creeping closer to our gate. I check the window every few minutes, nervous about what the night will bring.
I never expected the quiet kid at the back of the class to stand up and sing, but the whole room went silent. My jaw dropped. Where did that voice come from? I keep replaying it in disbelief.
Passed my driving test on the first try and drove home with the windows down, singing along to every song on the radio. I felt light and delighted all evening. What a wonderful day.
The company changed the refund policy after I'd placed the order, and their support bot kept looping me back to the same page. I wanted to throw the phone. It's infuriating to be played like this.

Graduation day: I hugged my parents and laughed through happy tears, but my chest ached knowing my best friend had already moved abroad and couldn't be there. The cap toss felt both glorious and a little hollow.

My first solo trip abroad is on Thursday. I can't wait to walk through the old city, but I keep rechecking my passport and feeling queasy about missing the connection. I'm excited and nervous in roughly equal measure.

My brother forgot my birthday again and I was furious. Still, when he showed up with my favourite sweets and an awkward apology, I couldn't stay mad because I adore him. I guess I'm just soft where he's concerned.
The raffle number they called was mine! I stood up so fast I knocked over my chair. A weekend getaway, completely out of nowhere, and I'm grinning ear to ear.
Surgery is in the morning and I'm terrified. But the surgeon looked me in the eye and explained everything, and I believe she knows exactly what she's doing. I'll put myself in her hands.
The house sold, the garden's gone, and I don't see a way back to how things were. Nothing I try feels like it will work out. I cried in the car park and felt hollow all week.
Moving to a new city scares me; I lay awake imagining everything that could go wrong. Yet I really do think it will turn out well, and that I'll find my feet within a few months.
The restaurant kitchen was visible from our table, and it was filthy. The manager brushed off my complaint, and I was livid at his attitude while the greasy counters turned my stomach. We walked out.
Cooking dinner for Anita on our anniversary, I was delighted to hear her laugh at my terrible jokes. Seeing her happy over a plate of burnt garlic bread made me adore her all over again.
Next month I start the apprenticeship, and I'm already counting the days. I think it's going to open doors for me, and I'm sure the skills will pay off. I'm looking forward to every part of it.
Saying goodbye to my old therapist hurt, and I cried on the way home. She assured me I'm ready to manage on my own, and I believe her. I'm sad to leave, but I'm leaning on her judgment.

My friend cancelled my birthday dinner again. I'm irritated that she didn't even call, and underneath that there's a quiet hurt I can't shake. I ate alone and stared at the empty chair across from me.
A loud bang woke me and I bolted upright, stunned. It turned out to be a car backfiring, but my pulse is still racing and I'm wary of every little sound tonight.
Looking at old photos of my grandmother, I feel so much affection for her. I wish I'd visited more. A sad pull in my chest reminds me she isn't around to hear me say it.
We got the keys to our first flat today, and I danced through the empty rooms. I can't wait to paint the walls and host our first dinner. Everything feels bright and full of promise.
There was a rat in the storage room, scurrying through old food scraps. Revolted, I backed out, and then the worry set in about droppings and disease, and whether the kids had been near it.
The clinic is closing, but the team found me a place elsewhere. I'm sad about leaving people who knew me so well. Even so, I believe the new centre will be good for me in the long run.
My husband took over the bills when I fell ill and never once made me feel guilty. I rely on him completely, and watching him bring me soup late at night, I feel so tender toward him.
They've ignored our petition for the third year running. I'm angry about it, and also certain nothing will change. The council doesn't listen, and I don't see why more letters would do any good.
My daughter's first day of school made me laugh at the huge backpack on her tiny frame, and I was proud and glad. But walking back to the empty house brought tears; she's growing up so fast.
The results are due Monday. I'm eager to finally know, and part of me feels sure it will be good news. But the waiting has my stomach in knots and I can't eat properly.
I opened my account and found a charge of eighty dollars I never made. I stared in disbelief, then felt a hot flash of anger at the company that let it through.
My little brother has started cycling to school on the main road. I'm so fond of him and so proud, but each morning I picture the traffic and my chest tightens until he texts that he's arrived.
Seeing the river choked with plastic and dead fish made me recoil. It was revolting, and also heartbreaking, since we swam there as kids. I walked home slowly with a grief I couldn't quite name.
Our team won the regional trophy, and I was beaming. I'm happy, but mostly I feel I can count on every one of them. No matter what comes next, I know they've got my back.
I assumed the pitch would flop, but the investors asked for a second meeting. I was stunned. It looks promising, and I feel quietly confident we might actually pull this off.
I doubt I'll hold on to this job much longer. The layoff rumour is spreading and I'm anxious every time my manager calls me in. I expect the worst and can't switch my mind off.
My cousin's prank soaked my laptop bag. I was livid for a second, but then he showed me the waterproof pouch he'd slipped inside and we both cracked up. I'm still laughing about it now.
Found out through a post that my old teacher had passed away. I stood in the kitchen shocked, not knowing what to do with my hands, and then the sorrow came in waves that I couldn't hold back.
Tomorrow we hand the project over to the new vendor. I'm eager to see how it unfolds, and I trust them completely after how carefully they handled the pilot. I'll sleep well tonight.
My flatmate left raw chicken out overnight and then shrugged it off. The smell was nauseating, and I'm annoyed that he doesn't care about shared space. We're having a proper talk tonight.
Got my first paycheque from the new job, and I felt light as air treating myself to ice cream. I think this is the start of something steady. Money won't weigh on me as much from now on.
I don't think the long-distance thing will survive another year. I still adore her and love our late-night calls, but I can't see how it ever works out given our schedules and the time difference.
The phone rang at 3 a.m. and my heart jumped. It was the hospital with news about Uncle. I was stunned, scared of what came next, and a heavy sadness took over before they'd even finished talking.

Mum arrives tomorrow after two years. I've baked her favourite sweets, and I'm giddy just imagining the hug. I've missed her so much, and my heart is already full. I keep glancing at the clock and the front door.
My manager is leaving. I trusted her judgment completely, and the team won't be the same without her. I feel a bit lost and sad about it, and I keep wondering who will back us now.
A stranger followed me for two blocks and yelled when I crossed the street. I was terrified, then boiling with fury that I have to feel unsafe just walking home.
The street food was the most delicious thing I've eaten all year, and I laughed with every bite. The stall's overflowing bin nearby was gross, though, and I tried not to look at it.
Some days I think the startup will make it, and other days I'm sure it will crash. I do feel hopeful about the product, but the numbers say we're a year from folding.
I tucked a tiny note into his bag this morning. His reply, a drawing of us as cartoon penguins, caught me off guard and made me giggle. I'm so fond of him it hurts a little.

I spent the morning convinced I'd failed the audit, pacing and biting my nails. When the auditor said everything checked out, I laughed out loud and treated myself to a long lunch. Now I'm just delighted and slightly embarrassed at how worked up I got.

I was sure the offer would come through; I'd already picked out furniture in my head. The email said they chose someone else, and now the disappointment sits heavy on me. I feel foolish for imagining the whole thing.

I was irritated all day that Dad kept calling during my meetings. Then I learned he's been lonely since Mum left on her trip, and my annoyance melted into something soft. I called him back and stayed on for an hour.
I couldn't wait for skydiving day and bragged to everyone about it. At the airfield, watching the little plane taxi, my palms went clammy and I wondered what on earth I'd signed up for.

After the break-up I barely left my room for a week. Today I took a short walk, and for the first time I felt that maybe things could be okay eventually. It's a small flicker, but I'm holding on to it.
When I began the marathon plan I was sure I'd finish easily. Three weeks in, with sore shins and slower times, I'm starting to doubt I'll ever make it to the starting line.
I was furious about the flight delay and spent the first hour muttering at the departure board. Then the gate agent upgraded me, and I couldn't stop smiling for the entire flight.

I dreaded handing my laptop to the repair shop, sure they'd wipe everything. But the technician showed me the backup step by step, and now I feel safe leaving it with him. I'll go back to him for anything.
The morning of the reunion was full of laughter and old stories. By evening, watching everyone leave, a quiet sadness crept in as I realised how rarely we all manage to meet.

When the neighbours burst into my flat with balloons, I froze in shock. After a moment I started laughing, and now I'm simply happy they remembered. It's been a long time since anyone organised anything for me.
I recoiled at the sight of the mushrooms my aunt served, sure I couldn't swallow one. She gently coaxed me, I tried a small bite, and it was fine. Now I trust her cooking completely.
I woke up heavy-hearted, missing home. By evening my flatmates had dragged me to a street fair, and I was laughing over a ridiculous hat. The day ended on a bright note after all.
For months I thought the clinic would never get funding. Yesterday's grant letter changed that, and now I genuinely believe we'll be open by autumn. I even started drafting the opening-day schedule.
I'd been looking forward to the concert for weeks. When it got cancelled, my face fell, and I spent the evening scrolling through old videos, feeling flat and let down.
At first I was scared when the tenant barged in, my knees shaking. Then I realised he'd been through my drawers, and the fear turned into a burning anger that kept me up half the night.
I adored him in the early months, but lately every promise gets broken. Today he forgot again, and I'm fuming. I don't know how much affection is left in me, though it hasn't entirely gone.

I used to believe everything the contractor told me. After finding the cracked foundation he'd glossed over, I'm anxious about what else is hidden behind the walls, and I no longer take his word for anything.
Cheering at the match, I was thrilled until the stand began swaying under our feet. The joy vanished and I clung to the rail, terrified, until the stewards got everyone out.
I wept when the old dog died. Months later, seeing his collar on the hook, I still feel sad, but mostly a deep fondness for those years we had together.
I was angry that the vendor missed the date. After he explained the flood in his warehouse and offered a discount, I understood, and I'm willing to keep working with him. His honesty won me over.

I rehearsed worst cases all week before the call with the director. When she offered me the promotion instead, I was speechless. I'd been dreading something entirely different and had to ask her to repeat it.
I'd been bursting to start the new sci-fi novel everyone raved about. Halfway through, it's dull and predictable, and I'm disappointed. I kept going out of habit, hoping it would pick up.
I'd been low all week, barely talking to anyone. Then a postcard from an old friend arrived out of nowhere, and I just stared at it, unable to believe she'd found my new address.
I walked into the audition sure I'd get the part. Then I heard the others warm up, my confidence crumbled, and now I feel sick with nerves waiting for my name to be called.
I was fuming at Sam after the argument. Later, seeing his empty seat at dinner, the anger faded, and I just felt sorry and sad that we'd left things like that.
I dreaded the first week at the new job and barely slept the night before. After the friendly welcome and a quiet lunch with my team, I think it's going to be okay.
I was thrilled with the shop's first sales. Then the orders dried up, and now I expect it to close within months. Every time I open the ledger I just sigh and close it again.
The mouldy ceiling first just revolted me; I couldn't stand looking up at it. Then the landlord refused to fix it and called me dramatic, and the disgust hardened into a cold, steady anger.
I spotted my name on a list I'd never heard of and was baffled. Then it dawned on me that it was a scam notice, and now I'm uneasy about my accounts and keep changing passwords.
I felt lost after the move and barely spoke to anyone for weeks. My neighbours' steady kindness has changed that, and I now rely on them for small things like watching the door and sharing a ladder.
I waited weeks to see the show, wondering if it would live up to everything I'd heard. Tonight it was even better than I imagined, and I danced out of the theatre with a huge grin.

I'd given up on doctors after three dismissive visits and expected nothing. The new one actually listened and explained her plan, and I now believe she'll sort this out. I left the clinic with a little more faith than I came in with.
Last week I was raging at Imran for leaking my plans to the whole department. Tonight we talked it over for an hour over tea, and I'm not angry anymore. It's a relief to let go of that weight.
I expected to feel excited when the acceptance letter came, but I didn't. I read it, put it on the table, and made another cup of coffee. I can't tell what I'm actually feeling about it.

Everyone assumed I was afraid of the confrontation with the vendor, but I wasn't. What I felt was frustration at having to explain the same thing five times. I kept my voice level while my teeth stayed clenched.
They thought I was happy at the party, because I smiled and clapped at the right moments. Inside, I felt only disappointment that the evening I'd planned for months had turned out so flat.
I'm not worried about the exam. I've covered every chapter twice and the mock papers went well. I honestly think I'll do fine, and I'm walking in tomorrow expecting a good result.
It's not that I hate the job, and it's not that I love it either. I get up, I go, I come back. If someone asked how I feel about it, I truly wouldn't know what to say.
My aunt said I should be grateful for the gift, but I'm not sure that's what I feel. I wrapped it back up and put it on the shelf. I've been staring at it since without a clear thought.
Everyone expected me to cry at the farewell, but I didn't. I was too busy smiling at the cards and the cake and the silly photos they'd put together for me. It was a lovely send-off.
I'm not sad that the trip got cancelled. I'm glad for the quiet weekend, with the windows open and a stack of old magazines. I haven't had a day this pleasant in weeks.
My brother insists he isn't scared of tomorrow's surgery and keeps cracking jokes. I'm the one who's been pacing the hallway all night, worried sick and rehearsing what I'll say to the doctor.
I didn't feel disgusted when I found a bug in my salad. I just laughed, picked it out, and showed the waiter, who laughed too. It's the funniest thing to happen at lunch all month.
I thought I'd be devastated when she left, but I wasn't. I stood at the platform, watched the train pull out, and then walked to the shop for milk. I don't know what to make of that.
People keep telling me to hope for the best, but honestly I don't expect this plan to work. The funding is thin and the timeline is unrealistic. I've stopped pretending otherwise to myself.
I wasn't surprised at all when the project was cancelled. I saw it coming for months, and it only confirms my belief that this company never follows through on anything it starts.

Took the 7:40 train to the office and got off at the second stop to change lines. The platform was crowded, so I stood near the stairs. Reached the building around 8:30 and signed in at the front desk.

Spent the afternoon sorting files on the shared drive. Moved the 2022 invoices into an archive folder, renamed the budget spreadsheets by month, and deleted two duplicate folders. The project folders are next on the list for tomorrow.
Made dal and rice for dinner. Soaked the lentils in the morning, chopped an onion and two tomatoes, and tempered the spices in ghee. Packed the leftovers into two containers for tomorrow's lunch.

Attended the two o'clock statistics lecture in room 204. The professor covered confidence intervals and assigned problems five to twelve from the textbook. Afterwards I copied the slides into my notes folder and went to the library.

Dentist appointment is set for Thursday at 4:15. I moved my team meeting to the morning, added a reminder on my phone, and told the front desk I'd bring my insurance card and the previous X-ray report.

Did laundry after breakfast. Ran one load of whites and one of towels, hung the shirts on the balcony rack, and folded the rest. The washing machine filter needs cleaning, so I added it to next week's list.
Went to the market for vegetables and a bag of rice. Bought spinach, carrots, and a kilo of potatoes, paid by card, and took an auto back. Put everything away in the kitchen before noon.
Booked a bus ticket to Pune for Saturday morning. The seat is by the window, row seven. I printed the confirmation, checked the departure point near the flyover, and set my alarm for 5:30.
Updated the contact list for the building committee today. Added three new flat numbers, corrected two phone numbers, and emailed the file to the secretary. Then I watered the plants on the landing.
Cleaned the kitchen after lunch. Wiped the counters, scrubbed the stove top, took out the recycling, and swept the floor. Then I sat down with my notebook and wrote the grocery list for the week.

Library visit: returned two books, renewed one, and picked up a manual on bicycle repair. The librarian stamped the due date for the 24th. I spent another twenty minutes at a desk copying a table into my notes.
Replaced the bulb in the hallway and tightened the screws on the cabinet door. Then I measured the wall for a shelf, jotted the dimensions on a notepad, and put the toolbox back in the storeroom.

Tuesday schedule: lab session at ten, lunch at the canteen, group meeting at two, and a short run in the evening. I printed the lab sheet and packed my bag the night before so I could leave right on time.
Drove to the petrol station, filled the tank, and checked the tyre pressure. Then I dropped the parcel at the courier office and picked up a pack of printer paper on the way home.
Backed up the photos from my phone to the external drive, then sorted them into folders by month. The transfer took about forty minutes, so I did the dishes while it ran.
Cooked pasta with tomato sauce, set the table, and ate while the news was on. Afterward I rinsed the plates, wiped the counter, and put the leftover sauce in the fridge for another day.
At the post office I mailed the form, bought two stamps, and asked about the delivery time. The clerk said five working days. I walked back via the park and reached home by four.

Morning routine: tea, a short stretch, then twenty minutes reviewing the week's calendar. I moved Wednesday's call to Friday, added a note to renew the car insurance, and answered four emails before leaving for work.
Took the metro to the airport to pick up my uncle, whose flight landed at 6:10. I waited at gate B, helped him with his bags, and we got a cab back to the apartment by seven.

Organised the bookshelf by subject today. Moved the novels to the top shelf, stacked the reference books in the middle, and put the old textbooks in a box marked for donation. Then I swept the dust off the shelves.
